doc.title: Vince Lateano interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Playing with Chet Baker at Kimballs
summary: A story of Chet's unpredictable behavior, brilliant playing and his cult following.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Right. You’ve got an awful long list of people you’ve played with or recorded with and I just wondered about a few of them. Chet Baker?

Well Chet was a gypsy. He’d come here and go there and do this and when he came to the Bay area, like a lot of people — another benefit of living here is that people do come through here and I get to play with them. But Chet was one of them. He was a character. A very good musician, very natural. I don’t think he ever practiced or really worked at it. I think he just had it. I don’t know. But he obviously had his — how do I put this — his agenda.

Yeah. And that was — I mean I saw him way down and way up. I mean I’ll never forget one time we were playing a club here called Kimballs, a nice little club behind the Symphony Hall. And we met, we played a weekend, Friday and Saturday, and we met at 4:00 or something for a sound check get together, you know, one of those, rhythm section. So we show up, it’s raining. And Chet shows up and he’s got like an Army jacket on and some old cords and shower shoes. And he shows up and we gave him a, “You want to play the blues?” He says, “Oh great, I’ll see you later.” And that was fine, because he was very spontaneous. That was 4:00. We come back at 9:00 and he’s sitting at the bar in the same outfit, you know in other words he hadn’t gone anywhere. And he was a little wasted. And he apologized. And we said well you do what you gotta do, just don’t fall off the stage. And the first set was pretty squirrelly. And it got better. And by the end of the night it was brilliant.

You know? I mean it was like amazing, how anybody could pull that off. He might have had some help you know, but it was like going in and thinking oh this is going to be a disaster. People are waiting in the rain to come in, like because he — another thing about working with Chet was he had — people came to hear him that you never saw anywhere in a jazz club. You know what I mean?

I guess not. It was like a cult or something. It was like he had a different kind of a following. I mean the usual jazz fan that you’ve seen at other concerts might be there. But then there were always people that he sort of brought out. And the next night he shows up © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

in a suit and all dressed up and looking totally different. And he even gave us extra money at the end of it. So you never knew what to expect. But I liked playing with him. He really was so lyrical, so pretty.
Sometimes it seems like the general audience likes their jazz musicians to be characters or somewhat tortured or something.
Like we would never be like that but we like to see someone.
